subject: Abruzzo and Erickson (1977)
object: Abruzzo and Erickson (1977) described a new syndrome characterized by cleft palate, coloboma, hypospadias, deafness, short stature, and radial synostosis.

subject: Abruzzo and Erickson (1977)
object: Abruzzo and Erickson (1977) concluded that the family history suggested either autosomal dominant inheritance with limited expression in females or X-linked inheritance.

subject: Davenport et al. (1986)
object: Davenport et al. (1986) described the external ear anomalies of CHARGE syndrome: short, wide pinnae that were often cupped and asymmetric; a distinctive triangular concha; a break between the antihelix and antitragus; and 'snipped-off' portions of the helical folds. The authors stated that these patterns were distinctive enough that a preliminary diagnosis of CHARGE syndrome could often be made from ear shape alone.

subject: Metlay et al. (1987)
object: Metlay et al. (1987) reported a boy with CHARGE syndrome. He had a coloboma of the optic nerve head and a congenital heart defect (atrial septal defect, ventricular septal defect and parachute mitral valve). He also had choanal atresia, severe growth retardation, genital hypoplasia, abnormal ears, cleft lip and palate, and pectus carinatum. His chromosomes were normal, and he died at 19 months of age; autopsy findings were reported.

subject: Metlay et al. (1987)
object: Metlay et al. (1987) noted that the mother of the affected boy was short and had hearing impairment, choanal atresia, and a coloboma. The authors suggested that this was evidence for dominant transmission of the disorder in this family, and they reviewed other familial cases from the literature.

subject: Abruzzo and Erickson (1989)
object: Abruzzo and Erickson (1989) did a follow-up study of the family they had previously reported with a new syndrome of cleft palate, coloboma, hypospadias, deafness, short stature, and radial synostosis. The purpose was to assess how the patients had developed since then and to determine whether they had CHARGE syndrome.

subject: Abruzzo and Erickson (1989)
object: Abruzzo and Erickson (1989) noted that other reports had cited their family as an example of familial CHARGE syndrome. After the follow-up study, they concluded that the patients in this family did not have familial CHARGE syndrome or the CHARGE association.

subject: Pauws et al. (2013)
object: In a family with X-linked CHARGE-like Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome of unknown cause, Pauws et al. (2013) found a novel TBX22 splice acceptor mutation (c.593-5T>A) that segregated with the phenotype. In silico analysis predicted that the variant abolishes normal mRNA splicing, and an in vitro splicing assay suggested that alternative splice sites were likely to be used. The authors concluded that TBX22 is the gene underlying Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome.

subject: Pauws et al. (2013)
object: Pauws et al. (2013) noted that the phenotype in the family with X-linked CHARGE-like Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome goes beyond classic X-linked cleft palate (CPX) to include sensorineural deafness and coloboma. These features had not previously been reported in CPX patients but are consistent with the developmental expression pattern of Tbx22.

subject: Pauws et al. (2013)
object: Pauws et al. (2013) found a novel TBX22 splice donor variant (c.767+5G>A) and a previously known canonical splice donor mutation (c.767+1G>A), both affecting the same exon as the Abruzzo-Erickson mutation, in patients with classic X-linked cleft palate. In silico and in vitro splicing studies predicted that both variants disrupt normal splicing.
